events.title: Jwalapuram (Kurnool): life before and after the Toba eruption
events.summary: Middle Palaeolithic stone tools at Jwalapuram in Kurnool district are found both below and above the ash of the Toba super-volcano (c. 74,000 years ago).
events.detail: The Jurreru valley at Jwalapuram preserves a thick bed of ash from the eruption of Toba in Sumatra. Tools of similar type above and below the ash suggest that people lived through the disaster. The Kurnool caves (Billa Surgam, Betamcherla) also have Stone Age bone tools and animal remains.
outcomes: Evidence that early humans in south India survived the Toba eruption.
facts: Robert Bruce Foote explored the Billa Surgam caves in Kurnool in the 1880s.

Billa Surgam caves are in Kurnool district (not Anantapuramu); the Belum caves (Nandyal district) are the second longest caves in India; the Kurnool caves and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi are the only places in India with upper palaeolithic bone tools (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Neolithic ash mounds of the southern Deccan
events.summary: From about 3000 BCE Neolithic cattle-herders of the southern Deccan leave huge ash mounds from burnt cattle dung, as at Utnur (Mahabubnagar) and Budihal (Karnataka).
events.detail: These pastoral communities of the Krishna–Tungabhadra region used polished stone axes, kept cattle in pens and periodically burnt the dung. Other Neolithic sites in Andhra and Telangana include Palavoy (Kurnool) and Veerapuram.
outcomes: Shows a cattle-based Neolithic culture in the south.
events.yearHook: c. 3000 BCE — when the Harappans were on the eve of their cities.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Harappan trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha)
events.summary: Mesopotamian texts from about 2350 BCE mention contact with "Meluhha", probably the Harappan region, which sent carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and wood (NCERT).
events.detail: Harappan seals, weights, dice and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, and a Persian Gulf seal at Lothal. The Mesopotamian texts call Meluhha "a land of seafarers"; the Harappans traded through Oman (Magan) and Bahrain (Dilmun) (NCERT).
facts: Copper from Oman has traces of nickel similar to Harappan objects (NCERT).
events.yearHook: c. 2350 BCE — Sargon of Akkad's time.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"

events.title: Megalithic burials in south India and Andhra
events.summary: From about 1000 BCE people in the Deccan and south India bury their dead in megaliths (big stones) with iron tools and black-and-red pottery (NCERT).
events.detail: Megaliths include stone circles, dolmens and cists; the dead were buried with pots, iron weapons and ornaments. NCERT notes that from c. 1000 BCE such burials were found across the Deccan, south India, the north-east and Kashmir, and that the goods buried showed differences in status. Andhra sites include Yeleswaram, Nagarjunakonda and Kadambapur.
outcomes: Iron came to the south with these communities.
facts: Some burials had more goods than others — a sign of social difference (NCERT).

Megalithic burials in Andhra: Tirupati has the largest anthropomorphic burial collection; sarcophagus burials are more common in Chittoor and Anantapuramu; Krishna and Chittoor have many dolmens; cyst burials are NOT most common in Visakhapatnam (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.yearHook: c. 1000 BCE — the same time as the Later Vedic age.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Persians conquer Gandhara
events.summary: Darius I of Persia conquers Gandhara and the Indus region around 518 BCE; it becomes the 20th and richest province of the Achaemenid empire.
events.detail: The Behistun inscription of Darius lists Gandhara and Hindush. The Persian contact brought the Kharosthi script (written right to left) and the Aramaic language to the north-west, and Indian soldiers fought in Persian armies against the Greeks.
outcomes: Taxila grew as a centre of learning.
events.yearHook: c. 518 BCE — about 200 years before Alexander.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha
events.summary: Soon after the Buddha's death a council of monks meets at Rajagriha under Ajatashatru's patronage and Mahakassapa's presidency to collect his teachings.
events.detail: Upali recited the rules of the order (Vinaya Pitaka) and Ananda the discourses (Sutta Pitaka), according to Buddhist tradition. The Buddha's teachings were passed on orally and written down much later; the Tipitaka has three "baskets" (NCERT).
outcomes: Vinaya and Sutta Pitakas compiled orally.
facts: The Tipitaka has three baskets: Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma (NCERT).
events.yearHook: The year the Buddha died, c. 483 BCE.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh); NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"

events.title: Bindusara succeeds Chandragupta
events.summary: Chandragupta Maurya abdicates and becomes a Jaina monk; his son Bindusara becomes emperor (c. 297 BCE).
events.detail: Bindusara is said to have extended the empire into the Deccan. He kept contact with the Seleucids; Deimachus came as ambassador. His son Ashoka was governor of Ujjain and Taxila before winning the succession.
outcomes: Ashoka succeeded him after a struggle (c. 268 BCE).
events.yearHook: c. 297 BCE, between Chandragupta (321) and Ashoka (268).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Kharavela of Kalinga and the Hathigumpha inscription
events.summary: Kharavela, the Jaina king of Kalinga, records his reign year by year in the Hathigumpha ("elephant cave") inscription at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar (c. 1st century BCE).
events.detail: The inscription says he repaired a canal first dug by a Nanda king, sent his army west against the Satavahana Satakarni, and attacked Magadha, bringing back a Jaina image taken by the Nandas. The Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves were made for Jaina monks.
outcomes: Kalinga became a strong Jaina kingdom.
events.yearHook: c. 1st century BCE — about 200 years after Ashoka's Kalinga war.

participants.role: The Nandas had dug the canal and taken the Jaina image.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: The Ranigumpha cave at Udayagiri is the finest of the Jaina caves.

events.title: Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription
events.summary: The Shaka ruler Rudradaman I records in Sanskrit (c. 150 CE) that he repaired the Sudarshana lake, built under Chandragupta Maurya and improved under Ashoka (NCERT).
events.detail: It is the first long inscription in chaste Sanskrit. It says a storm broke the dam and the king repaired it from his own treasury without forced labour or extra taxes (NCERT). He also claims to have twice defeated Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha, but spared him because of a relationship.
outcomes: Sanskrit became the language of royal inscriptions.
facts: The same rock has an Ashokan edict.
Shaka rulers: Maues (Moga), Azilises, Chastana (Ujjain), Nahapana and Rudradaman; Suvishakha was Rudradaman's Pahlava governor who repaired the dam.
Shaka rulers took the titles Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa.
Parthians (Pahlavas): Gondophernes (Gondophares) — Takht-i-Bahi inscription (45 CE); St Thomas came in his time.
events.yearHook: c. 150 CE — the same century as Gautamiputra.

participants.role: The lake was built in his time (NCERT).
The lake was improved in his time (NCERT).
Repaired the lake again in the 5th century.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"

events.title: Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya
events.summary: In 499 CE Aryabhata, aged 23, writes the Aryabhatiya at Kusumapura (Pataliputra), stating that the earth rotates on its axis and explaining eclipses (NCERT).
events.detail: He gave the place-value system a firm base, a value of pi close to 3.1416, and rules for squares, cubes and roots. He said day and night were caused by the earth's rotation and that eclipses happen because of the shadows of the earth and moon, not because of Rahu (NCERT). Varahamihira (Panchasiddhantika, Brihatsamhita) and Brahmagupta came later.
outcomes: Basis of Indian astronomy; India's first satellite named after him (1975).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Vakatakas and the Ajanta paintings
events.summary: Under the Vakataka king Harishena (c. 460–478 CE) many of the Ajanta caves are cut and painted with scenes from the Jatakas (NCERT shows Ajanta paintings).
events.detail: The Vakatakas ruled the Deccan and were allies of the Guptas: Chandragupta II's daughter Prabhavati married Rudrasena II. Ajanta has 29 rock-cut Buddhist caves; the paintings in caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 are the finest. The site was rediscovered by a British officer in 1819.

alsoOn.text: Ajanta caves rediscovered by a British officer, John Smith.

events.yearHook: c. 475 CE, between Fa-Hien (405) and Aryabhata (499).

participants.role: His daughter married into the Vakataka family.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Hunas and Yashodharman
events.summary: The Huna (White Hun) kings Toramana and Mihirakula conquer the north-west; Yashodharman of Malwa defeats Mihirakula around 528 CE, as his Mandsaur pillar records.
events.detail: Skandagupta had pushed back an earlier Huna attack (c. 455–460 CE). Toramana conquered Punjab and Malwa about 500 CE. His son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala and persecuted Buddhists. Gupta power broke up under the strain.
outcomes: Decline of the Guptas; rise of regional kingdoms (Maukharis, Pushyabhutis).

participants.role: Had held back the first Huna attack.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Salankayanas of Vengi
events.summary: After the Ikshvakus, the Salankayanas rule from Vengi (near Eluru) in the Krishna–Godavari delta (c. 300–440 CE); their king Hastivarman is defeated by Samudragupta (Prayaga prashasti).
events.detail:
They issued copper-plate charters in Prakrit and later Sanskrit and worshipped Chitraratha Swami (the Sun). The Brihatphalayanas (Kudura) and Anandagotrikas (Guntur) were small dynasties of the same age. Vengi later became the capital of the Eastern Chalukyas.

The early Pallavas also ruled parts of southern Andhra, issuing Prakrit charters such as the Mayidavolu plates of Shivaskandavarman; Vishnugopa of Kanchi was another king defeated by Samudragupta.
outcomes: Followed by the Vishnukundins; Vengi became the Eastern Chalukya capital.
events.yearHook: c. 300–440 CE: between the Ikshvakus and the Vishnukundins.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: The Manchikallu and Maidavolu (Mayidavolu) inscriptions belong to the Pallavas (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Simhavishnu revives the Pallavas of Kanchi
events.summary: Simhavishnu (c. 575) ends the Kalabhra interlude and makes the Pallavas of Kanchi a great power; his son Mahendravarman I and grandson Narasimhavarman I fight the Badami Chalukyas (NCERT notes the rise of the Pallavas c. 500–600).
events.detail: The early Pallavas had issued Prakrit charters from the Andhra region. Kanchi became a great centre of learning (the ghatika). The Pallavas spread the Grantha script and Indian culture to Southeast Asia. The Cholas ended Pallava rule (c. 897).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Later Pallavas: Nandivarman II built the Vaikuntha Perumal temple, Kanchi; Aparajitavarman was the last, defeated by the Cholas.
Mahendravarman I defeated Pulakeshin II at Pullalur (by Pallava claim).
